data.cultural_impact: The name Adiarth carries a deep sense of reverence for ancient wisdom and cultural traditions. It reflects a strong connection to one's heritage, and the name itself becomes a constant reminder of the importance of preserving and passing down the knowledge and values of the past. In a broader sense, it celebrates the importance of tradition and the wisdom that comes from it, making for a name that is deeply rooted in Indian culture.
data.spiritual_significance: In Spiritual terms, the name Adiarth holds great significance as it represents the primordial source of knowledge, consciousness, and existence. Adi (the beginning) signifies the origin of all things, while Arth (meaning or goal) reflects the ultimate reality and consciousness that lies beyond the material world. Thus, the name Adiarth invokes a sense of deep spirituality, reminding us to search for the ultimate source of all knowledge and wisdom. It is a name that encourages introspection, self-awareness, and enlightenment, inspiring those who bear it to seek a deeper understanding of life and the universe.

historical_references.reference: Adiarth was a legendary king of the Lunar Dynasty, also known as the Soma or Suryavansha dynasty, in ancient India. He is said to have ruled during the late Imbuke or early Bhagiratha period, around 1100 BCE. Adiarth is best known for his involvement in the Churning of the Ocean of Milk (Samudra Manthan), an epic event in Hindu mythology where the gods and demons worked together to obtain the elixir of immortality (amrit). The churning was facilitated by the cosmic serpent Vasuki, who was used as a rope to pull the mountain Mandara back and forth. Adiarth held the mountain on his head during this process, thereby providing crucial support and ensuring the event's success.
historical_references.time_period: Late Imbuke or early Bhagiratha period, around 1100 BCE

historical_references.reference: Adiarth is also mentioned in the Mahabharata, an ancient Indian epic, as the father of Bhishma Pitamaha, the grandsire of the Pandava and Kaurava princes. In this context, Adiarth is described as a warrior king and a descendant of the lunar deity Chandra. He is said to have ruled over the kingdom of Hastinapura, which was the capital city of the Kuru kingdom.
